title: Part 2, Chapter 2
paragraphs: "What if they've already searched the place? What if I find them in my room?"
But here was his room. Empty. No one had been in it. Even Nastasya hadn't touched anything. But God -- how could he have left all those things in the hole?

He rushed to the corner, slipped his hand behind the wallpaper, pulled the things out, and stuffed them into his pockets. There were eight items in all: two small boxes with earrings or something of the kind -- he barely looked; then four small leather cases. There was also a chain wrapped in newspaper, and something else in newspaper that looked like a medal or decoration.... He distributed them among the pockets of his overcoat and trousers, trying to make them as inconspicuous as possible. He took the purse too. Then he left his room, leaving the door open. He walked quickly and purposefully, and though he felt shattered, his mind was clear. He was afraid of pursuit, afraid that within the next half hour -- the next quarter hour, perhaps -- orders would be issued to track him down. He had to destroy all traces before then. He had to do it while he still had some strength, some capacity for reasoning left.... Where should he go?

That had been decided long ago: "Throw everything in the canal -- all traces gone in the water, end of story." He had decided this during his night of delirium, when he kept feeling the urge to get up and go, to hurry, to get rid of it all. But getting rid of it turned out to be much harder than he'd thought. He wandered along the Yekaterininsky Canal for half an hour or more, eyeing the steps that led down to the water, but he couldn't bring himself to do it. Either there were rafts moored at the steps where women were washing clothes, or boats were tied up and people were swarming everywhere. Besides, he could be seen from the embankments on all sides. It would look suspicious -- a man going down to the water on purpose, stopping, and throwing something in. And what if the boxes floated instead of sinking? They certainly would. As it was, everyone he passed seemed to be staring at him, turning to look, as if they had nothing better to do than watch him. "Why? Or am I imagining it?" he thought.

Finally it occurred to him that it might be better to go to the Neva. There were fewer people there, he'd be less conspicuous, and it would be more practical in every way -- plus it was farther from here. He wondered how he could have spent a good half hour wandering in this dangerous area, anxious and agitated, without thinking of that before. And he had wasted that half hour on an irrational plan simply because he'd conceived it in his delirium! He was becoming extraordinarily absent-minded and forgetful, and he knew it. He definitely had to hurry.

He walked toward the Neva along V----- Prospect, but on the way another idea struck him. "Why the Neva? Wouldn't it be better to go somewhere far off, to the islands again, and hide the things in some secluded spot -- in a forest, under a bush -- and mark the place?" And though he felt incapable of clear judgment, the idea seemed sound. But he was not destined to get there. Coming out of V----- Prospect toward the square, he noticed on the left a passageway leading between two blank walls into a courtyard. On the right, the bare, unplastered wall of a four-story building stretched deep into the yard. On the left, a wooden fence ran parallel to it for about twenty paces before turning sharply left. It was a deserted, fenced-off area littered with rubbish of various kinds. At the far end of the yard, the corner of a low, grimy stone shed peeked out from behind the fence -- probably a coachmaker's or carpenter's workshop. The whole area near the entrance was black with coal dust. "This would be the place to dump it," he thought. Seeing no one in the yard, he slipped in and immediately noticed near the gate a sink, the kind often found in yards with lots of workmen or cab drivers. On the fence above it, someone had scrawled in chalk the familiar wit: "No loitering." All the better -- nothing suspicious about him going in here. "I'll throw it all in a pile and get out!"

Looking around once more, his hand already in his pocket, he noticed a large, rough-hewn stone against the outer wall, between the entrance and the sink, weighing perhaps sixty pounds. On the other side of the wall was the street. He could hear passersby -- always numerous in this neighborhood -- but no one could see him from the entrance, unless someone came in from the street, which could easily happen. He had to be quick.

He bent down, gripped the top of the stone firmly with both hands, and using all his strength rolled it over. Under the stone was a small hollow in the ground. He immediately emptied his pockets into it. The purse sat on top, and the hollow still wasn't full. Then he gripped the stone again and with a single twist rolled it back into position, though it sat slightly higher than before. He scraped some dirt around it and pressed the edges down with his foot. Nothing was visible.

He went out and headed into the square. Once again an intense, almost unbearable joy swept over him for an instant, as it had at the police station. "I've buried my tracks! And who -- who would ever think of looking under that stone? It's probably been lying there since the building was built and will lie there just as many years more. And even if it were found, who would connect it to me? It's over! No evidence!" And he laughed. Yes, he remembered later that he started laughing -- a thin, nervous, silent laugh -- and went on laughing the whole time he was crossing the square. But when he reached K----- Boulevard, where two days earlier he had come upon the girl on the bench, his laughter abruptly stopped. Other thoughts crept in. He suddenly felt it would be revolting to walk past that bench where he'd sat and brooded after the girl left, and equally hateful to run into that mustachioed policeman he'd given twenty kopecks to. "Damn him!"

He walked on, looking around him angrily and distractedly. All his thoughts now seemed to be circling around a single point, and he felt there really was such a point, and that now -- right now -- he was standing face to face with it. For the first time, truly, in the last two months.

"Damn it all!" he thought suddenly, in a fit of uncontrollable rage. "If it's begun, then it's begun. To hell with the new life! God, how stupid it all is!... And the lies I told today! How pathetically I groveled before that miserable Ilya Petrovich! But that's all nonsense! What do I care about any of them, or about my groveling! That's not it at all! Not it at all!"
He stopped suddenly. A new, utterly unexpected, and extremely simple question had struck him, leaving him baffled and bitterly confounded.

"If this whole thing was really done deliberately and not like an idiot, if I really had a definite purpose, then how is it that I never even looked inside the purse and don't know what I got -- what I went through all this agony for, what I deliberately undertook this vile, filthy, degrading act for? And just now I was about to throw the purse into the water along with everything else, without even looking at it... How is that possible?"

Yes, that was how it was. All exactly so. And yet he had known this before -- it wasn't a new question for him -- even when he had decided in the night, without hesitation or deliberation, as though it had to be that way, as though it couldn't be otherwise.... Yes, he had known it all and understood it all. It had surely been settled yesterday, at the very moment he was bending over the strongbox and pulling out the jewel cases.... Yes, exactly so.

"It's because I'm very sick," he finally decided grimly. "I've been tormenting myself, working myself into a frenzy, and I don't know what I'm doing.... Yesterday and the day before and all this time I've been driving myself crazy.... I'll get well and stop worrying.... But what if I don't get well at all? God, I'm so sick of all of it!"

He kept walking without rest. He desperately wanted some kind of distraction but didn't know what to do, what to try. A new, overpowering sensation was taking hold of him more completely with every passing minute: an immeasurable, almost physical revulsion for everything around him -- a stubborn, malignant hatred. Everyone he met disgusted him -- their faces, their movements, their gestures. If anyone had spoken to him, he felt he might have spat in their face or bitten them....

He stopped suddenly as he came out on the bank of the Little Neva, near the bridge to Vasilyevsky Island. "He lives here, in that building," he thought. "So I haven't come to Razumikhin on purpose? It's the same thing again.... Very interesting, though -- did I come here deliberately or did I just wander here by accident? Never mind. I said the day before yesterday that I'd go see him the day _after_ -- well, here I am! Besides, I really can't walk any farther."
He went up to Razumikhin's room on the fifth floor.

Razumikhin was home in his garret, writing at that moment, and opened the door himself. It had been four months since they'd seen each other. Razumikhin was sitting in a tattered dressing gown, slippers on bare feet, uncombed, unshaved, unwashed. His face registered surprise.

"Is that you?" he cried. He looked his friend up and down; then after a brief pause, whistled. "Things that bad? You've outdone even me, brother!" he added, taking in Raskolnikov's rags. "Come on, sit down -- you must be exhausted."
When Raskolnikov sank onto the American leather sofa, which was in even worse shape than his own, Razumikhin immediately saw that his visitor was sick.
"You're seriously ill -- you know that?" He began feeling his pulse. Raskolnikov pulled his hand away.
"Never mind," he said. "I came to... I have no lessons.... I wanted, but... I don't really want lessons...."
"Listen, you're delirious!" Razumikhin said, watching him carefully.
"No, I'm not."

Raskolnikov got up from the sofa. Climbing the stairs to Razumikhin's, he hadn't realized how much he dreaded coming face to face with his friend. Now, in a flash, he understood that what he wanted least in the entire world at this moment was to be face to face with anyone. Bile rose inside him. He nearly choked with rage at himself the instant he crossed Razumikhin's threshold.
"Goodbye," he said abruptly, and walked toward the door.
"Wait, wait! You strange creature."
"I don't want to," the other said, pulling his hand away again.
"Then what the hell did you come for? Are you out of your mind? This is... almost insulting! I'm not letting you go like this."

"Fine, then -- I came because I know no one but you who could help... to start... because you're kinder than anyone -- smarter, I mean -- and can think things through... and now I see I don't need anything. Do you hear? Nothing at all... nobody's help... nobody's sympathy. I'm on my own... alone. Enough. Leave me alone."

"Hold on, you lunatic! You're absolutely raving. Do what you want, for all I care. Listen -- I don't have any teaching work either, and I don't care, but there's a bookseller named Kheruvimov, and he's as good as a whole batch of lessons. I wouldn't trade him for five. He does a kind of publishing -- puts out natural science pamphlets -- and what sales they get! The titles alone are worth the price! You always said I was a fool, but believe me, brother, there are bigger fools than me! Now this Kheruvimov has decided to be progressive -- not that he understands the first thing about it, but I encourage him naturally. Here are two printer's sheets of a German text -- in my opinion, the crudest charlatanism. It discusses the question 'Is Woman a Human Being?' and, of course, triumphantly proves that she is. Kheruvimov is going to publish this as a contribution to the women's question. I'm translating it. He'll stretch the two and a half sheets to six, we'll slap on a gorgeous half-page title, and sell it for fifty kopecks. It'll go! He pays me six rubles a sheet, which comes to about fifteen for the whole thing, and I've already had six in advance. When we finish this, we're starting on a translation about whales, and then some of the most tedious gossip from Part Two of the _Confessions_ -- we've already marked the passages. Somebody told Kheruvimov that Rousseau was a kind of Radishchev. I certainly don't contradict him -- to hell with him! So, do you want to do the second sheet of 'Is Woman a Human Being?' If you do, take the German text, some pens and paper -- they're all provided -- and take three rubles. Since I got six in advance for the whole thing, three of those are yours. When you finish the sheet, there'll be another three rubles. And don't think I'm doing you a favor -- on the contrary, the moment you walked in I saw how you could help me. First, my spelling is terrible, and second, my German sometimes goes completely off the rails, so I mostly just make things up. The only consolation is that it's probably an improvement. Though who knows -- maybe sometimes it's worse. Will you take it?"

Raskolnikov silently took the German pages, took the three rubles, and without a word walked out. Razumikhin stared after him in astonishment. But when Raskolnikov was on the next street, he turned back, climbed the stairs to Razumikhin's again, laid the German article and the three rubles on the table, and left once more, still without a word.
"Have you lost your mind, or what?" Razumikhin shouted, finally furious. "What kind of game is this? You'll drive me crazy too... What did you come here for, damn it?"
"I don't need... any translation," Raskolnikov muttered from the staircase.
"Then what the hell do you need?" Razumikhin yelled from above. Raskolnikov continued descending in silence.
"Hey! Where do you live?"
No answer.
"Then to hell with you!"

But Raskolnikov was already on the street. On the Nikolaevsky Bridge he was jolted back to full consciousness by an unpleasant incident. A coachman, after shouting at him two or three times, gave him a vicious crack across the back with his whip -- he had nearly walked under the horses' hooves. The lash so enraged him that he leapt toward the railing (for some unknown reason he had been walking right down the middle of the bridge, in the thick of traffic). He clenched and ground his teeth in fury. He could hear laughter, of course.
"Serves him right!"
"Pickpocket, I bet."
"Pretending to be drunk, most likely, throwing himself under the wheels on purpose -- and then you're the one who has to answer for it."
"It's a whole profession, that's what it is."

But as he stood at the railing, still angry and bewildered, watching the retreating carriage and rubbing his back, he suddenly felt someone press money into his hand. He looked. It was an elderly woman in a headscarf and goatskin shoes, accompanied by a girl -- probably her daughter -- wearing a hat and carrying a green parasol.
"Take it, my good man, in Christ's name."

He took it and they walked on. It was twenty kopecks. From his clothes and appearance, they had probably taken him for a beggar -- and the gift was no doubt inspired by the lash of the whip, which made them feel sorry for him.

He closed his hand around the twenty kopecks, walked on about ten paces, and turned to face the Neva, looking toward the palace. The sky was cloudless and the water almost bright blue -- a rare sight on the Neva. The cathedral dome, seen at its best from this spot on the bridge about twenty paces from the chapel, glittered in the sunlight, and in the clean air every ornament on it was clearly visible. The sting of the lash faded, and Raskolnikov forgot about it. A single troubled, not quite definable thought now occupied him completely. He stood still and gazed long and intently into the distance. This spot was deeply familiar to him. When he was at the university, he had stood here hundreds of times -- usually on his way home -- staring at this truly magnificent view, almost always marveling at the vague and mysterious feeling it stirred in him. It had always left him strangely cold; this gorgeous panorama was somehow blank and lifeless for him. He had always wondered at this dark, enigmatic impression, and, not trusting himself, kept putting off any explanation. Now he vividly recalled those old doubts and perplexities, and it struck him as no accident that he was recalling them now. It seemed strange and grotesque that he should have stopped at the same spot as before, as if he actually imagined he could think the same thoughts, be drawn to the same ideas and images that had occupied him... so short a time ago. He found it almost amusing, and yet it wrung his heart. Deep down, hidden far away out of sight, all of that seemed to belong to the past now -- all of it: his old thoughts, his old questions and theories, his old impressions, that panorama, and he himself, and everything.... He felt as though he were rising into the air and everything were fading from view. Making an unconscious movement with his hand, he suddenly noticed the coin in his fist. He opened his hand, stared at it, and with a sweep of his arm flung it into the water. Then he turned and headed home. He felt as though he had cut himself off from everyone and everything at that moment.

It was evening by the time he got home, so he must have been walking for about six hours. How or by what route he returned, he couldn't remember. He undressed, trembling like an exhausted horse, lay down on the sofa, pulled his overcoat over himself, and immediately sank into oblivion....
He was awakened at dusk by a terrible scream. My God, what a scream! He had never heard such unnatural sounds -- such howling, wailing, grinding, tears, blows, and curses.

He could never have imagined such brutality, such frenzy. He sat up in bed in terror, nearly fainting from anguish. But the fighting, wailing, and cursing grew louder and louder. Then, to his intense amazement, he recognized his landlady's voice. She was howling, shrieking, and wailing -- rapidly, frantically, incoherently -- so that he couldn't make out what she was saying. She was begging, clearly -- begging not to be beaten, for she was being beaten mercilessly on the stairs. Her attacker's voice was so horrible with spite and rage that it was more of a rasp than a voice, but he too was saying something, just as fast and unintelligibly, rushing and sputtering. Suddenly Raskolnikov began to tremble. He recognized the voice -- it was Ilya Petrovich's. Ilya Petrovich was here, beating the landlady! He was kicking her, slamming her head against the steps -- that was clear from the sounds, the cries, the thuds. How could this be? Had the world turned upside down? He could hear people running from every floor and every staircase -- voices, exclamations, knocking, doors slamming. "But why, why -- how is this possible?" he kept repeating, seriously thinking he had gone mad. But no, he could hear it all too clearly! And then they would come for him next. "Because obviously... it's all about _that_... about yesterday.... My God!" He wanted to bolt his door, but he couldn't lift his arm... and besides, it would be pointless. Terror gripped his heart like ice, tortured him, numbed him.... But finally, after about ten minutes, the uproar gradually began to subside. The landlady moaned and groaned; Ilya Petrovich still made threats and cursed.... But at last he too seemed to fall silent, and then he was gone. "Has he really left? Dear God!" Yes, and now the landlady was leaving too, still weeping and moaning... then her door slammed.... The crowd was dispersing from the stairs back to their rooms -- exclaiming, arguing, calling to one another, their voices rising to shouts, dropping to whispers. There must have been a great many of them -- practically everyone in the building. "But, God, how can this be? And why -- why had he come here?"

Raskolnikov sank back onto the sofa, drained, but couldn't close his eyes. He lay there for half an hour in such anguish, such an unbearable sensation of infinite terror, as he had never known before. Suddenly a bright light filled his room. Nastasya came in with a candle and a plate of soup. After looking at him carefully and determining he was not asleep, she set the candle on the table and began laying out what she'd brought -- bread, salt, a plate, a spoon.
"You haven't eaten since yesterday, I'll bet. You've been wandering around all day and you're burning up with fever."
"Nastasya... why were they beating the landlady?"
She looked at him intently.
"Who beat the landlady?"
"Just now... half an hour ago. Ilya Petrovich, the assistant superintendent, on the stairs.... Why was he doing that to her, and... why was he here?"
Nastasya studied him silently, frowning. The scrutiny went on for a long time. He felt uneasy, even frightened by her searching gaze.
"Nastasya, why aren't you saying anything?" he asked timidly at last, in a weak voice.
"It's the blood," she finally answered softly, as though talking to herself.
"Blood? What blood?" he mumbled, going white and turning toward the wall.
Nastasya continued to look at him without speaking.
"Nobody has beaten the landlady," she declared at last, firmly and resolutely.
He stared at her, barely able to breathe.

"I heard it myself.... I wasn't asleep... I was sitting up," he said, even more timidly. "I listened for a long time. The assistant superintendent came.... Everyone ran out onto the stairs from every apartment."
"Nobody's been here. That's the blood crying out in your ears. When it has nowhere to go and starts clotting, you begin seeing things.... Are you going to eat something?"
He didn't answer. Nastasya stood over him, watching.
"Give me something to drink... Nastasya."
She went downstairs and came back with a white ceramic jug of water. He remembered only swallowing one sip of cold water and spilling some on his neck. Then came oblivion.
